quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The movie I watched last night was terrifying. What has happened to the relative clause in this sentence?
quests.targetClause: The relative pronoun has been left out because the clause describes an object.
quests.completedSentence: The movie I watched last night was terrifying. What has happened to the relative clause in this sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I watched' already has its own subject ('I'), so 'the movie' is the object of 'watched.' Object relative pronouns like 'that' can be omitted, which is exactly what happened here - the full version would be 'The movie that I watched...'
quests.nativeTip: Try inserting 'that' or 'which' right after 'movie' - does the sentence still make the same sense? Then ask what role 'the movie' plays inside that added clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The relative pronoun has been left out because the clause describes an object."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence has its relative pronoun omitted?
quests.targetClause: The dish I ordered arrived cold.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence has its relative pronoun omitted?
quests.ruleExplanation: In 'The dish I ordered arrived cold,' the object relative pronoun has been dropped entirely - 'I ordered' follows 'the dish' with no connector, which is only possible for object relative clauses.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the sentence where a noun is directly followed by a subject and a verb, with no connecting word in between.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The dish I ordered arrived cold."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence means exactly the same thing as: 'The song that she recorded became a hit'?
quests.targetClause: The song she recorded became a hit.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence means exactly the same thing as: 'The song that she recorded became a hit'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The song she recorded became a hit' keeps the exact same meaning: 'that,' the object relative pronoun, is simply dropped, since 'the song' is the object of 'recorded' and 'she' remains the clause's subject.
quests.nativeTip: Removing the pronoun should not remove any other information - check that both 'she' and 'recorded' are still there.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The song she recorded became a hit."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence below is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: The man who works at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence below is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: Because 'the man' is the subject of 'works' (there's no other candidate), the relative pronoun cannot be omitted - it must stay, and since he's a person and the subject, 'who' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: This clause needs its own subject - the gap itself must supply it here, so nothing can be left out.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The man who works at the pharmacy is my neighbor."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which version below is the grammatically correct one?
quests.targetClause: The man I met at the pharmacy is my neighbor.
quests.completedSentence: Which version below is the grammatically correct one?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I' is the subject of 'met,' so 'the man' is the object - an object relative pronoun here, so it can be dropped entirely, giving 'The man I met...'
quests.nativeTip: Check whether the clause already has its own subject elsewhere ('I') - if so, the object pronoun can safely disappear.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The man I met at the pharmacy is my neighbor."

quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: The article ___ criticized the new policy sparked a huge backlash.
quests.targetClause: that
quests.completedSentence: The article that criticized the new policy sparked a huge backlash.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Criticized' has no other subject - 'the article' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped here. Since it's a thing acting as the subject, 'that' is required.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'criticized' already has a subject somewhere else in the sentence.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with which
quests.questionSentence: Which version of this sentence is NOT grammatically acceptable?
quests.targetClause: The policy whom the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash.
quests.completedSentence: Which version of this sentence is NOT grammatically acceptable?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' can only refer to people, never things, so 'The policy whom the senator criticized...' is ungrammatical. The other three are all acceptable: the object relative pronoun can be 'that,' 'which,' or simply omitted.
quests.nativeTip: Three of these are simply different valid ways to express the same object relative clause - only one breaks a basic rule.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The policy whom the senator criticized sparked a huge backlash."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Formal: 'This is the gift that my sister gave me.' Which casual rewrite keeps the same meaning and is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: This is the gift my sister gave me.
quests.completedSentence: Formal: 'This is the gift that my sister gave me.' Which casual rewrite keeps the same meaning and is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This is the gift my sister gave me' is the natural, casual version: the object relative pronoun 'that' is simply dropped, while 'my sister gave me' keeps its normal subject-verb-object order.
quests.nativeTip: Removing the connector shouldn't scramble the rest of the sentence - the subject and verb inside the clause should stay in their normal order.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "This is the gift my sister gave me."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: Casual: 'The guy I talked to seemed nice.' Which is the more formal, fully-written version?
quests.targetClause: The guy whom I talked to seemed nice.
quests.completedSentence: Casual: 'The guy I talked to seemed nice.' Which is the more formal, fully-written version?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' is the formally correct object pronoun for a person; restoring it reproduces the same meaning as the casual, omitted version.
quests.nativeTip: Restoring the missing pronoun means adding back a word - and since the antecedent is a person in object position, only one option fits both criteria.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The guy whom I talked to seemed nice."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence best matches this meaning: 'I finally found my keys. I had lost my keys last week.'?
quests.targetClause: I finally found the keys I had lost last week.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence best matches this meaning: 'I finally found my keys. I had lost my keys last week.'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I finally found the keys I had lost last week' correctly omits the object relative pronoun while keeping 'I' as the clause's subject and using the correct past perfect tense, 'had lost,' to show the losing happened before the finding.
quests.nativeTip: Check that the clause still has its subject and the correct verb tense, even without a connecting pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I finally found the keys I had lost last week."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which of these versions breaks a basic grammar rule?
quests.targetClause: This is the man whose I met at the wedding.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these versions breaks a basic grammar rule?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' must be immediately followed by the noun it possesses (like 'whose car'); it cannot stand alone as a direct object the way 'whom,' 'who,' or an omitted pronoun can.
quests.nativeTip: Three of these express the same idea in different registers - only one breaks a basic grammar rule about what this pronoun can do.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "This is the man whose I met at the wedding."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: This is the man ___ I met at the wedding. Which option would sound most natural if you were casually telling a friend this story out loud?
quests.targetClause: (leave it out entirely)
quests.completedSentence: This is the man (leave it out entirely) I met at the wedding. Which option would sound most natural if you were casually telling a friend this story out loud?
quests.ruleExplanation: In casual spoken English, the object relative pronoun is very often dropped entirely - 'This is the man I met at the wedding' - making omission the most natural, casual choice, even more common than 'who.'
quests.nativeTip: Think about how briefly people actually speak in casual storytelling - what's the shortest natural option?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "(leave it out entirely)"

quests.nativeTip: This sentence is from a formal, written email - check which object pronoun fits that register best.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The photos from our trip I finally uploaded last night turned out beautifully. What is the true antecedent of the omitted relative clause 'I finally uploaded last night'?

quests.completedSentence: The photos from our trip I finally uploaded last night turned out beautifully. What is the true antecedent of the omitted relative clause 'I finally uploaded last night'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I uploaded' the photos, not the trip itself; 'from our trip' is just a prepositional phrase describing which photos, so 'the photos' is the true antecedent of the omitted object relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: Ignore 'from our trip' for a moment - what did 'I' actually upload?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the photos"
